Which Orlando resorts charge resort fees?

Most large Orlando hotels near the theme-park corridor charge some form of daily resort or amenity fee, while many condo-style and vacation-package stays do not. A resort fee is a mandatory nightly charge stacked on top of the room rate to cover amenities the property bundles together, whether or not you use them. It is not a tax and not a tip, and it is set by the property, so two hotels on the same street can charge very different amounts.

The honest answer to "how much" is a range, not a fixed number: across the Orlando market these fees are commonly reported between $15 and $45 per night. Rather than publish specific hotel dollar amounts that go stale within weeks, we track the package price of Orlando deals directly. Our tracked Orlando inventory averages $258 with entries from $49 across 181 deals, and the strongest values are packages that fold amenities into one upfront number.

How do you check the exact Orlando resort fee before booking?

Verify the fee on the property's own reservation page, not a third-party summary, because that is the only figure that is contractually current. Three reliable steps: (1) run a dummy booking to the final price screen where mandatory fees must be itemized under U.S. all-in pricing rules; (2) read the "fees and policies" or "property details" section for the words "resort fee," "amenity fee," or "destination fee"; (3) if it is still unclear, call the front desk and ask "what is the total mandatory nightly charge beyond the room rate and tax?"

Key fact: A resort fee is charged whether or not you use the amenities it bundles. If a property advertises a low nightly rate but adds a $40 resort fee, the real cost is the rate plus $40 plus tax — always compare on the out-the-door total.

A vacation package deposit is the money you pay to lock in the offer, and the key question is whether it is refundable and under what conditions. How much tax is on a $99 vacation package?

On a $99 room-based package, expect roughly $10 to $18 in combined lodging tax, because U.S. hotel taxes stack state sales tax, county/city lodging tax, and tourism-district levies into a combined rate that commonly lands between 10% and 18%. Bottom Line Up Front: A vacation deal's sticker price is the starting line: resort fees, taxes, parking, and add-ons can push the out-the-door cost 20-60% higher. What's the difference between sticker price and out-the-door cost?

The sticker price is the advertised headline; the out-the-door cost is what you actually pay after every mandatory fee and tax. The two diverge because U.S. lodging pricing lets a property advertise a low room rate and recover margin through a resort fee, taxable on top, plus parking, and optional add-ons that feel mandatory in the moment. A package that quotes a single all-in price collapses that gap, which is why comparing on the out-the-door total — not the headline — is the only honest way to rank deals. This page is the master hub every other fee page links to.

Our tracked data anchors the comparison: 617 active deals, average $301, median $199, average price-per-night $94, and 168 deals under $100. Those are one-time package prices, so the out-the-door math is mostly tax plus any property fees, not a second nightly fee.

Worked example: what a $99 deal really costs

Take a $99 headline. If it is an all-in package in a 13% tax market with free parking and included WiFi, the out-the-door cost is about $112 — the sticker plus tax, full stop.
